first_impression.reaction: The headline 'You Did Not Know?' is clickbait and nearly lost me. But the opener goes straight to a correction: 'They don't.' Three countries, three rulebooks. That's a factual claim, not a sales pitch. I jumped to the FAQ, saw short dated answers with embassies named, then went back up.

journey.section: Baltic wedding traditions: three countries, three sets of customs
journey.quote: Where a custom is passed on by word of mouth rather than documented, we say it is "often told", and we leave its meaning to your family.
journey.reaction: Good. They tell me upfront which bits are sourced and which are folklore. I can check the encyclopedia and UNESCO bits myself.

journey.quote: Most of what follows comes from the Visuotinė lietuvių enciklopedija, Lithuania's national encyclopedia, and describes historic village custom; today's couples choose which parts to keep.
journey.reaction: Named source, and honest that it's historic, not what every wedding does today. That's the kind of limitation I want stated.

journey.quote: It is the custom couples are least likely to drop. The planner LRT interviewed in 2015 said couples rarely give up being met at the reception with salt, bread and water.
journey.reaction: That's a sweeping claim resting on one planner's comment from eleven years ago. Either say 'one planner said in 2015' and stop there, or show me something newer.

journey.quote: How a Kihnu wedding runs today is often told rather than recorded.
journey.reaction: Same as last time: 'often told' turns up in nearly every section. I get the disclaimer, but by the fifth time it reads like a verbal tic.

journey.quote: Not as wedding customs on their own. UNESCO's entries for Kihnu (Estonia), the Suiti cultural space (Latvia) and sutartinės (Lithuania) name weddings among their traditions or themes.
journey.reaction: They didn't overclaim the UNESCO angle. Most sites would say 'UNESCO-listed wedding traditions'. Dates of inscription, links to the entries. I'll check, but I expect it holds up.

journey.quote: [Latvia](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/destinations/europe/latvia) is "Exercise normal safety precautions" overall, with "Reconsider your need to travel" for areas near the border with Belarus (updated 2 June 2026).
journey.reaction: Dated, linked, and they flag the awkward bit instead of burying it under the headline rating. Exactly right.

journey.section: Paperwork and which embassy to ask
journey.quote: There is no Australian embassy in any of the three countries.
journey.reaction: Useful and blunt. Plus the bit about Warsaw being appointment-only and Vilnius doing no notarial acts. Real friction points, stated plainly.

journey.section: Paperwork and which embassy to ask
journey.quote: Ask it whether it issues a CNI for a wedding in Estonia or Latvia.
journey.reaction: So they don't actually know whether Stockholm issues the CNI. Honest, but it's the one practical answer I came for and it's handed back to me.

journey.section: Bringing Baltic customs to a wedding at home
journey.quote: One person is your single point of contact, and the fee and inclusions are agreed in writing before any work begins. The legal and church steps stay with the registry, your church and the embassy.
journey.reaction: Fee and inclusions in writing, and they say what they don't do. Good. Still nothing on whether they take a cut from suppliers.

unanswered_questions: Does Wedded Wonderland take commissions or mark-ups from venues and vendors?
What does the Wedded Advisor fee cover and how is it calculated?
Have they actually planned a wedding in Riga, Vilnius or Tallinn, or a Baltic-Australian one? A real example with the budget would help.
Can they source a Latvian folklore group for mičošana, in the Baltics or in Australia, or is that on us?
Does the Stockholm or Warsaw embassy actually issue the CNI for these countries?

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the Baltic Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: Clickbait headline. The article is better than its title.

turn_offs_found.quote: If you would like help shaping it, in Riga, Vilnius, Tallinn or at home, a conversation with a Wedded Advisor is a calm place to start.
turn_offs_found.why: 'Calm place to start' is soft-sell. Tell me what the first conversation covers and whether it costs anything.

turn_offs_found.quote: A bread and salt welcome, a midnight mičošana or a private bonnet moment all travel well.

would_share_with: My partner, for the country-by-country breakdown and the embassy section
Her parents, to check which customs the family actually keeps

cta_reaction.quote: One person is your single point of contact, and the fee and inclusions are agreed in writing before any work begins.
cta_reaction.why: The CTA comes after the evidence, not before, and 'fee and inclusions in writing' is the right signal. I'd still look for a fees or commissions page before giving them my email.

top_3_changes: Retitle away from 'You Did Not Know?' to something factual, e.g. naming the three countries.
Soften 'It is the custom couples are least likely to drop' to match its single 2015 source, and cut 'all travel well' or back it up.
Reduce repeated 'often told' to one clear signpost per section, and swap 'a calm place to start' for what the first conversation actually covers.

No prices on the page is the house standard and not penalised.
